answer.rationale: The obvious reflex under a competitor price cut is promotional_pricing, and memory_73 endorses it ('strong acquisition and revenue lift'). But the recovered source exp_73 shows that summary is lossy in a value-relevant way: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% came with 30-day retention -12%, and the source explicitly concludes the discounted cohort does not survive first renewal and that discounting must NOT be generalized as sustainable growth. Against the stated objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue), promotional_pricing is disqualified — and matching a competitor's deeper cut would likely amplify exactly the churn we are trying to stop, buying vanity signups from the most price-elastic, least durable segment. Of the remaining options, only memory_86 is corroborated by a recovered source: exp_86 confirms completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. Retention lift is the correct lever against churn pressure, and faster time-to-value is a genuine defense against a price-based attack because it raises perceived worth rather than lowering price. memory_31 (signup field reduction) points the same direction and is cheap to bundle, though it is unverified. memory_57 (referrals) and memory_91 (activation messaging) are plausible but rest on uncorroborated summaries of the same kind that proved lossy for memory_73, so I will not lean on them today; memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) does not address the SMB base under attack and would be a segment change, not a response. Scale: standard_experiment, not broad rollout — the exp_86 evidence was gathered on self-serve accounts under normal conditions, not on a churning, price-shocked SMB cohort, so the +3% retention effect may not transfer at the same magnitude; I want a measured read before committing the base. Explicitly preserved uncertainty: onboarding improvement is unlikely to fully offset a deep competitor discount for the most price-sensitive accounts, and it is a slower lever than a price match. I accept that near-term signup numbers may look worse than the discount path; that is the intended trade. Next cycle's verification budget should go first to memory_57 and memory_91, since both are single-line optimistic summaries with no recovered source and both carry the same silent-harm risk pattern that memory_73 exhibited.
